# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

### Introduction and Historical Context
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has fundamentally reshaped the management of severe symptomatic aortic stenosis [11]. While standard transfemoral transarterial access is the preferred approach, approximately 10% to 15% of patients with severe aortic stenosis are unsuitable candidates for this route due to extensive peripheral arterial disease, heavy vascular calcification, severe tortuosity, or small-caliber iliofemoral arteries [12,14]. In the early days of TAVR, alternative routes were restricted to transthoracic options such as transapical or transaortic access [14]. However, these approaches carry high perioperative morbidity, prolonged recovery times, and increased mortality rates, especially in fragile, high-risk populations [14,15].

To avoid violating the thoracic cavity and to preserve the benefits of conscious sedation and rapid mobilization, peripheral alternative access methods have been developed [12]. These include transcarotid, transaxillary/subclavian, and transcaval access [12,15]. Transcaval (caval-aortic) access, first validated in preclinical animal models in 2013 [1] and successfully applied in humans in 2014 [2], creates a temporary percutaneous pathway from the femoral vein through the inferior vena cava (IVC) directly into the adjacent infrarenal abdominal aorta [13]. This pathway allows structural operators to bypass severely diseased iliofemoral arterial segments completely.

### Pre-Procedural Planning and Anatomic Suitability
An essential prerequisite for transcaval access is precise pre-procedural imaging planning [3]. Multidetector computed tomography (CT) remains the gold standard for evaluating candidate anatomy [3,6]. Key parameters assessed on CT include finding a calcium-free crossing target on the abdominal aortic wall that directly opposes the adjoining IVC, ensuring a trajectory free of intervening organs, bowel, or major side branches (such as lumbar or renal arteries) [6,10]. The spatial relationship between the IVC and aorta must be evaluated to identify the ideal puncture projection [10]. Modern CT mapping protocols also assess unique patient anatomy, such as the presence of abdominal aortic aneurysms or prior synthetic aortic grafts, which can still be navigated successfully using modified electrosurgical techniques [5,26,27].

### Technical Execution of Transcaval Access
The transcaval technique represents a premier application of transcatheter electrosurgery [22]. The procedure is performed under fluoroscopic and angiographic guidance in a hybrid catheterization laboratory [4,20]. First, a target snare is introduced through a secondary arterial access site and positioned in the abdominal aorta [4]. From the femoral vein, a guiding catheter is advanced into the IVC and aligned with the aortic snare under orthogonal fluoroscopic views [26]. A micro-guidewire is then electrified using standard hospital radiofrequency electrosurgical generators in monopolar mode, which vaporizes the adjacent tissue plane within milliseconds to allow seamless traversal from the IVC to the aorta [4,22]. Once captured by the aortic snare, the guidewire is externalized, allowing the introduction of a standard stiff wire and subsequent step-by-step dilation to accommodate large-bore delivery sheaths (typically 14-Fr to 20-Fr) [4,20].

### Clinical Efficacy and Comparative Safety
Although the creation of an iatrogenic aortocaval fistula may seem counterintuitive, its physiological safety is underpinned by the retroperitoneal space pressure dynamics [2,26]. Because the interstitial pressure of the retroperitoneal space exceeds venous pressure, any extravasated blood from the arteriotomy preferentially decompresses into the low-pressure venous sink of the IVC rather than causing retroperitoneal hemorrhage [2,26]. 

The landmark National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) prospective transcaval study demonstrated a 99% success rate for access and closure, with low rates of major vascular complications and no procedural mortality [9]. Multi-center registries in both North America [8] and Europe [18] have mirrored these outcomes, establishing transcaval access as a highly reproducible and safe alternative [6,23]. 

Furthermore, clinical comparisons from the STS/ACC TVT Registry have positioned transcaval TAVR as a compelling alternative to surgical approaches [15,25]. A propensity-weighted contemporary analysis of transcaval versus transaxillary TAVR showed that transcaval access was associated with a five-fold lower rate of stroke and transient ischemic attack (2.5% vs. 13.2%) [24]. This neuroprotective advantage is primarily because the transcaval route completely avoids the manipulation of the supra-aortic trunk vessels [15,28].

### Complications and Dedicated Closure Devices
Access-site complications of the transcaval approach include residual aortocaval fistulae, retroperitoneal hematomas, and vascular injuries [16,26]. Historically, closure of the caval-aortic puncture site was performed off-label using nitinol cardiac occluders, such as the Amplatzer Duct Occluder [16]. While these occluders achieved high long-term closure rates (93% at 12 months) [16], persistent early fistulae and minor bleeding remained common [16]. To address this gap, a dedicated, purpose-built transcaval closure device has been developed [17]. Preclinical and early human studies show that this dedicated device significantly improves immediate sealing and dramatically reduces the incidence of access-site bleeding [17,26].

### Expanding Indications
While primarily used for TAVR [8,9], transcaval access has successfully facilitated other large-bore endovascular interventions, such as thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) [7]. Most recently, it has emerged as a crucial approach for the percutaneous delivery of mechanical circulatory support (MCS) devices [29,30]. For instance, delivery of the 23-Fr Impella 5.0 microaxial flow pump via the transcaval route in patients presenting with cardiogenic shock has been shown to be feasible and safe, offering higher-flow left ventricular unloading while entirely bypassing the limb ischemia associated with traditional femoral arterial access [29,30].

### Conclusion
Transcaval access is a highly effective, percutaneous, neuroprotective alternative for TAVR and other large-bore structural heart interventions [21,28]. While requiring specialized training and meticulous pre-procedural planning [26,27], its clinical outcomes challenge the necessity of traditional surgical alternative access routes [19,28], solidifying its role in the contemporary structural heart team's vascular portfolio.
